title: Algebra 1: Introduction to Algebra

findings.finding: The tasks require zero for an absent requested coefficient or constant term, but neither convention is explained.
findings.breakdown: The definitions identify displayed multiplying numbers and terms without variables. They do not explain why an absent component has numerical value zero rather than the response 'none'.
findings.checked: The complete earlier teaching, coefficient demonstrations, constant-term demonstrations and p13 summary contain no explanation of either convention. Knowing multiplication by zero does not itself establish these identification conventions; practice answer explanations are not supplied teaching.
findings.assumptions: These algebraic identification conventions are new in this introductory booklet. Calculator use is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before p12-coefficient-m, add: 'If there is no x term, its coefficient is 0: y = 0x + y.' Before p12-constant-l, add: 'If no constant term is shown, the constant term is 0: 9y = 9y + 0.'

findings.doneWhen: Both zero conventions are explained before their first independent use.

history.note: Its comment was deleted in Studio.

Preserve the existing teacher rejection: the same absent-term convention finding was replayed after layout-only table consolidation changed target structure. No mathematics or teaching changed for those tasks.

findings.finding: Students must distinguish the coefficient of x from the coefficient of x² before the explicit explanation of that distinction.
findings.breakdown: In x² + 5x, recognising that both terms contain the pronumeral x does not establish that the request selects only the term with the specified power.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching explains repeated multiplication and identifying terms, but does not contrast coefficients of different powers. coefficient-power-drill-root supplies exactly that contrast later.
findings.assumptions: Selecting a coefficient by its requested power is new here.

repair.proposal: Move the explanatory sentences from coefficient-power-drill-root to immediately before p12-coefficient-t: 'In 3x² + 7x, the coefficient of x is 7, from 7x. The coefficient of x² is 3, from 3x². Match the requested power to its term.' Retain the later paired practice.

findings.doneWhen: The explicit power comparison precedes p12-coefficient-t.

findings.finding: Finding the coefficient of x in x² + 5x is repeated unchanged.
findings.breakdown: The later drill deliberately compares requested powers, but states no retrieval or comparison purpose for repeating the earlier whole task. Changing both later paired expressions preserves its comparison.
findings.checked: p12-coefficient-t and coefficient-power-drill-e have the same instruction, expression and requested coefficient. coefficient-power-drill-f shares the later expression and must change with it to protect the pair.
findings.assumptions: No additional purpose for repeating the earlier task is stated.

repair.proposal: Change coefficient-power-drill-e to 'Coefficient of x in x² + 6x' (answer: 6), and coefficient-power-drill-f to 'Coefficient of x² in x² + 6x' (answer: 1).

findings.doneWhen: The later pair retains its power comparison and hidden unit coefficient without repeating p12-coefficient-t.

findings.finding: Follow the existing constant-difference comparison by changing the multiplier from four to five.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the difference to the repeated copies of the constant inside brackets.
findings.checked: At a=2 the values are 13 and 25; at a=10 they are 53 and 65. Both differences are 12. Repeated-group interpretation and substitution are available; formal expansion is unnecessary.
findings.assumptions: 'Difference' means the positive difference, consistent with the existing question.

repair.proposal: Append after p33-q15-f: (g) 'When a=2, find the difference between 5a+3 and 5(a+3).' Answer: 12. (h) 'When a=10, find the difference between 5a+3 and 5(a+3).' Answer: 12. (i) 'Explain why changing a from 2 to 10 did not change this difference.' Expected answer: both expressions contain five lots of a; their remaining amounts are 3 and 15, giving a difference of 12.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts extend the existing comparison using numerical cases and one explanation.

findings.finding: Algebraic generalisation is requested before choosing and consistently reusing pronumerals is modelled.
findings.breakdown: Students must distinguish repeated occurrences of one varying number from two independently varying quantities. The introductory example supplies only an English rule.
findings.checked: p3-algebra and p3-generalising define pronumerals and generalisation but do not model this translation. The algebraic answers in p3-guided are student blanks. p16-information eventually explains consistent pronumeral use, but comes after these tasks.
findings.assumptions: This is the introductory teaching of algebraic generalisation. Calculator use is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Append to p3-example-demonstration: 'Let n represent any number. Replace the changing number with n and keep zero unchanged: n×0=0. Use the same letter whenever you mean the same number.' Before p4-q1-c, add: 'The numerator and denominator can vary independently, so use different letters: a/b=a÷b, where b is not zero.'

findings.doneWhen: Consistent reuse of one pronumeral and selection of distinct pronumerals are demonstrated before their first independent use.

history.note: Its comment was deleted in Studio.

findings.finding: Seven independently answered later parts repeat unchanged earlier tasks without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Each repeated part has the same expression and requires the same notation conversion. The surrounding mixed questions supply no stated purpose for exact repetition.
findings.checked: Compared all seven pairs, including their shared instructions, complete expressions and requested outputs. These are unchanged tasks, rather than merely repeated methods with different values.
findings.assumptions: Each separately labelled, independently answered part is a whole task.

repair.proposal: Replace later copies as follows: p10-q5-a: 7×m, answer 7m; p10-q5-b: 8×t, answer 8t; p10-q5-c: m×9, answer 9m; p10-q5-e: 11×w×w, answer 11w²; p10-q7-a: 7w, answer 7×w; p10-q7-c: tr, answer t×r; p10-q7-d: 6abc, answer 6×a×b×c.

findings.finding: Identifying the coefficient of a specified power is required before the linear and squared terms are distinguished.
findings.breakdown: The definition 'number multiplying a pronumeral' does not settle which term to select when both x and x² occur.
findings.checked: p6 teaches repeated multiplication and p11 teaches term boundaries, including expressions with different powers. Neither models matching a coefficient request to the specified power.
findings.assumptions: Prior polynomial coefficient instruction is not assumed.

repair.proposal: Before p12-coefficient-t, add: 'In 2x²+7x, the coefficient of x is 7, from 7x. The coefficient of x² is 2, from 2x². Match the requested power before reading its coefficient.'

findings.doneWhen: An explicit contrast distinguishes coefficients of linear and squared terms before independent identification.

history.note: Its comment was resolved in Studio.

findings.finding: Missing-part subtraction and equal-part division introduce unmodelled uses of bar diagrams.
findings.breakdown: Students must change from adding displayed parts to subtracting known parts from a whole or sharing a whole equally. Earlier teaching does not explain how the unknown's position determines this choice.
findings.checked: p16-guided-c–f teaches adjoining parts and their totals, which supports p19-q10-a. Earlier container questions also concern totals. No preceding explanation models an unknown remainder or an unknown equal share.
findings.assumptions: Numerical subtraction and equal sharing are prior knowledge; interpreting these algebraic bar relationships is the new component.

repair.proposal: Before p19-q10, explain: 'Aligned whole bars represent the same total. To find a missing part, subtract the known parts from the whole.' Model a whole t split into ? and 4, giving ?=t−4. Before p20-q11-c, model a whole w split into three equal unknown parts: each part=w÷3=w/3.

findings.doneWhen: Subtraction order and equal-share division are modelled before their independent use.

history.note: Its comment was deleted in Studio.

findings.finding: 'Divide into' introduces an unexplained reversal of division order.
findings.breakdown: Students may use the taught dividend-first interpretation of 'divided by' and select the reciprocal expression.
findings.checked: p21-operations-block explicitly explains subtraction reversal but supplies no 'divide into' wording. Earlier division tasks use 'divided by' or sharing.
findings.assumptions: This language variant has not been established in the supplied teaching.

repair.proposal: Before p27-q14, add: 'Divide u into v means v÷u. Compare: divide 2 by 10 gives 2/10; divide 2 into 10 gives 10/2.'

findings.doneWhen: The two division wordings are explicitly contrasted before matching.

history.note: Its comment was deleted in Studio.

findings.finding: Extend the bags-and-blocks comparison by connecting one additional bag to an equivalent number of loose blocks.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up makes the different quantities represented by a coefficient and a constant concrete.
findings.checked: The original diagram represents 5x+4. With six blocks per bag the totals are 34 and 40, so six loose blocks reproduce the increase. Numerical group totals are already practised in p17-q1–q3.
findings.assumptions: Each bag contains the same six blocks in the follow-up.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts after p18-q7-explanation: (a) 'Each bag contains 6 blocks. How many blocks are in the original diagram?' Answer: 34. (b) 'Add one more bag. How many blocks are there now?' Answer: 40. (c) 'Starting with the original diagram, how many loose blocks would you add to obtain the total in part (b)?' Answer: 6.

findings.doneWhen: The numerical follow-up uses the original diagram and distinguishes adding a bag from adding one loose block.

findings.finding: A fixed negative base with consecutive exponents would expose the alternating signs of its powers.
findings.breakdown: Only the exponent varies in the run, making its effect visible before a mixed follow-up.
findings.checked: For a=-2, powers two through five are 4, -8, 16 and -32. With c=-3 and b=6, c³+b=-21. Powers, negative substitution and signed multiplication are available by this topic.
findings.assumptions: Retain the existing assignments a=-2, b=6 and c=-3.

repair.proposal: After p40-q9-i add the single instruction 'Predict the sign before evaluating each power.' Under the existing evaluation instruction append j a²; k a³; l a⁴; m a⁵; then the unpatterned follow-up n c³+b. Answers: 4, -8, 16, -32, -21. The base stays fixed throughout j–m; only the exponent changes.

findings.doneWhen: The four-power run and mixed follow-up appear together, with only the one prediction instruction added.

findings.finding: Extend the 3x+1 table by relating a ten-unit input increase to its output increase.
findings.breakdown: The numerical comparison connects 'change by 3' to its stated meaning per unit increase in x.
findings.checked: 3(6)+1=19 and 3(16)+1=49, an increase of 30 across ten input units. p43-consecutive supplies the per-unit meaning. Placement is adjusted to preserve the consecutive table comparisons.
findings.assumptions: The follow-up remains attached to part b but is attempted after the existing table sequence.

repair.proposal: After all existing p44-q1 tables, append an optional follow-up referring back to part b: (i) 'For 3x+1, find the values when x=6 and x=16.' Answers: 19 and 49. (ii) 'How much has the expression value increased between these inputs?' Answer: 30. (iii) 'Explain why this increase is 30 although the table says “Change by 3”.' Expected answer: x increased by 10, giving ten increases of 3.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up connects input and output changes without interrupting the existing variation groups.

findings.finding: The scope of a power on a bracketed product is first required without being taught.
findings.breakdown: Students may interpret (ab)² as ab² because preceding power examples repeat individual pronumerals and do not contrast the two bases.
findings.checked: p6-indices-rule-block and p7-conventions demonstrate single-pronumeral bases. p6-brackets teaches multiplication next to brackets, including composite factors, but does not explain powers of those factors.
findings.assumptions: Numerical power notation is prior knowledge; its application to a composite algebraic base is a new variant here.

repair.proposal: Before p10-q6-f, add: 'A power after brackets repeats the whole bracketed base: (ab)²=(ab)×(ab). Compare ab²=a×b×b.'

findings.doneWhen: Students see the difference between squaring the whole product and squaring its final factor before attempting p10-q6-f.

history.note: Its comment was resolved in Studio.

findings.finding: A short comparison can expose which factors a square repeats.
findings.breakdown: Keeping the factors fixed makes exponent placement and scope easier to compare.
findings.checked: The proposed products are correct for all numerical a and b. They require multiplication notation, repeated multiplication and the bracketed-base teaching proposed for c3.
findings.assumptions: Place this after the bracketed-base explanation.

repair.proposal: After p10-q6, ask: 'Predict which factors occur twice, then write each expression as a product: ab; a²b; ab²; (ab)².' Expected products: a×b; a×a×b; a×b×b; (a×b)×(a×b). Keep a and b fixed while changing the square's placement and scope. Follow with the unpatterned item 3(cd)², giving 3×(c×d)×(c×d).

findings.doneWhen: The run includes prediction, comparison of the four products and an unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: The first fractional coefficient is stated without showing its origin as a multiplying number.
findings.breakdown: The definition asks students to identify a multiplier, but x/3 displays division. The example does not connect these representations.
findings.checked: p6-division-rule-block and p7-conventions connect division to fraction notation. Neither shows x/3=(1/3)x. Subsequent answer blanks do not supply the missing worked connection.
findings.assumptions: Elementary fraction arithmetic is prior knowledge. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before 'Coefficient is 1/3', insert: 'x/3=(1/3)×x, so the number multiplying x is 1/3.'

findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly identifies where the fractional multiplying number comes from.

findings.finding: Translating an operation on a whole sum or difference is required before the grouping decision is explained.
findings.breakdown: Students must construct an intermediate expression and preserve it as one operand. Knowing that adjacency to brackets means multiplication does not show when a verbal description requires those brackets.
findings.checked: p6-brackets-f–h uses already bracketed composite factors, so composite multiplication is not wholly absent. However, p21-write-group models only single-operation translations, and no earlier supplied teaching models constructing grouping from a whole-result description.
findings.assumptions: The issue is choosing grouping during translation, rather than recognising previously supplied brackets.

repair.proposal: Before p21-write-i, add: 'For “subtract 4 from n, then double the result”, first write n−4. Double the whole result: 2(n−4). Writing n−2×4 doubles only 4.' Also show: 'Square the sum of a and b: (a+b)². Divide that sum by 3: (a+b)/3; the fraction bar groups the whole numerator.'

findings.doneWhen: Students see how a whole-result description determines an intermediate expression and its grouping before independent translation.

history.note: Its comment was resolved in Studio.

findings.finding: The opening example uses multiplication before addition without an opening review of that numerical decision.
findings.breakdown: A left-to-right evaluator can substitute correctly but then calculate the wrong total. Naming order of operations does not rehearse the choice.

findings.finding: Distinguish agreement at one input from equivalence for every input.
findings.breakdown: This develops the equivalence comparison already requested in p35-q19.
findings.checked: At n=2, n² and 2n both give 4; at n=3 they give 9 and 6. The expressions 5n/2 and 5(n/2) agree for every real n by associativity of multiplication with 1/2. No variable denominator restricts their domain.
findings.assumptions: A numerical counterexample and a verbal multiplication explanation are sufficient.

repair.proposal: After p35-q19, offer: 'At n=2, compare n² and 2n. Are they equivalent? Find an input that settles your answer. Then explain why 5n/2 and 5(n/2) are equivalent without relying on one substituted value.' Expected answer: the first pair is not equivalent, since n=3 gives 9 and 6. The second pair both multiply n by 5 and by 1/2, in either grouping.

findings.doneWhen: Students distinguish a counterexample from an explanation valid for every input.

history.note: Its comment was resolved in Studio.

findings.finding: The negative-substitution examples combine signed multiplication, addition and subtraction without an opening review of those operations.
findings.breakdown: Correct substitution still requires evaluating 4(−2), 10+(−8) and 12−(−15). Errors in these prerequisite operations obstruct the new substitution method.
findings.checked: p37 has no review. The preceding exercise contains isolated negative results and some negative inputs, but does not practise these signed operations throughout or rehearse subtraction of a negative. Exponent scope is removed from this finding because p31-q8-k–m and later preceding practice already contrast coefficient and bracketed bases.
findings.assumptions: Signed arithmetic is prior learning, consistent with Computation with Integers in the course library. Short recall questions assume no calculator.

repair.proposal: Before p37-information, ask: '(a) Evaluate 7+(−3), 3+(−7), −4+(−2). (b) Evaluate 3×(−4), (−3)×4, (−3)×(−4). (c) Evaluate 8−(−2), −5−(−3), 2−5.' Expected answers: (a) 4, −4, −6; (b) −12, −12, 12; (c) 10, −2, −3. These nine short calculations fit within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The teacher can check signed addition, multiplication and subtraction before the examples require them.

findings.finding: Explain how the parity of a positive integer power affects the sign of a negative input.
findings.breakdown: The task generalises the square and cube substitutions through repeated multiplication.
findings.checked: For t>0, even positive integer powers of −t equal those of t; odd positive integer powers are their negatives. The explanation uses previously taught repeated multiplication and signed products.
findings.assumptions: Restrict the generalisation to positive integer powers.

repair.proposal: After p40-q9, offer: 'Let t>0. Compare (−t)² with t² and (−t)³ with t³ using products. Predict the relationships for powers 4 and 5. What determines whether changing the input's sign changes the answer's sign?' Expected answer: even powers agree; odd powers have opposite signs. Pairs of negative factors give positive products, while an odd count leaves one unpaired negative factor.

findings.doneWhen: The explanation connects the sign pattern to paired negative factors.

history.note: Its comment was deleted in Studio.

findings.finding: Construct a generating expression from its starting value and constant change.
findings.breakdown: This reverses the topic's existing interpretation of coefficient and constant.
findings.checked: 7−3x and −3x+7 give 7 at x=0 and decrease by 3 for each unit increase in x. In general dx+s starts at s and changes by d. Substitution and equal-group reasoning suffice.
findings.assumptions: Use consecutive nonnegative integer inputs for the pattern; s and d may be real numbers.

repair.proposal: After p46-q3-l, offer: 'A pattern starts at 7 when x=0 and decreases by 3 whenever x increases by 1. Write two forms of an expression and explain why both work. Generalise to starting value s and change d.' Expected answer: 7−3x and −3x+7; generally dx+s.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain separately how the constant fixes the starting value and the coefficient fixes the change.

history.note: Its comment was deleted in Studio.

findings.finding: Extend the existing comparison by adjusting the constant so the paired expressions agree.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up uses the same expressions and inputs to connect the observed difference with the amount contributed by five lots of 3.
findings.checked: For a = 2, 5(a + 3) = 25, so the missing constant is 15. At a = 10, both expressions give 65. The explanation continues the reasoning already requested in p33-q15-i and requires no formal expansion algorithm.
findings.assumptions: Students can describe multiplication as equal groups, as established earlier.

repair.proposal: After p33-q15-i, add optional parts: j. 'When a = 2, complete 5a + □ = 5(a + 3).' Answer: 15. k. 'Use your completed expression when a = 10. What value does each side give?' Answer: 65 on each side. l. 'Explain why your chosen number works for both values of a.' Expected answer: both expressions contain five lots of a, and five lots of 3 contribute 15.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up retains the existing numbers and separates completion, evaluation and explanation into individual parts.

history.note: New optional follow-up after the approved g–i extension. Kept separate from the repaired finding whose generated ID was reused.

contextQuestions.question: Before these tasks, have students learned to undo successive operations in reverse order, including equations such as 4−3x=4/7, and to recover two unknowns from paired outputs such as a+b=10 with a+2b=17 or a+b=7 with a−b=13? The booklet includes missing-input practice but no supplied explanation of these methods; whether the separately taught equation topics precede this booklet would change the assessment.
